facts.F2: Mr. Harilela let the premises to Kwan Kau for a period of 2 years and 5 months commencing from 1st December 1966.

facts.F4: On 15th June 1968, Mr. Harilela re-entered upon the whole of the ground floor in exercise of his powers under clause 5(a) of the lease.
facts.F5: Mr. Harilela wrote to each of the defendants on 17th June 1968, stating that they would become his tenants for the residue of the term of the lease i.e., up to the 30th day of April 1969.

facts.F9: On 16th May 1969, the defendants applied to Mr. Justice McMullin for a mandatory order to open the entrances to the arcade, but their applications were refused.
facts.F10: The defendants regarded the letter of 17th June 1968 as a notice to quit and had said so in their pleadings.

facts.F3: On the 15th August 1985, the plaintiff entered into a contract for one year with the defendant to print cancellation bulletins.
facts.F4: The contract was renewed on the 15th May 1986 for two years and again for a further period of two years on the 15th November 1988, expiring on the 31st December 1990.
facts.F5: When the contract with the plaintiff was renewed in November 1988, Mr Fellman, a Vice-President of the defendant, was responsible for obtaining quotations for the printing of the cancellation bulletins.
facts.F6: Mr Antony Fung was employed by the defendant as a manager under Mr Fellman and liaised with Mr Wong in connection with the requirements of the defendant for the printing of the cancellation bulletins.
facts.F7: On the 22nd August 1988, Mr Wong wrote to the defendant with regard to a renewal of the contract and requested a revision of the previous pricing arrangement on the grounds of an increase in mailing costs and additional handling charges.
facts.F8: It is alleged by the defendant that the grounds for the increase were spurious and were made as a result of a collusive agreement between Mr Wong and Mr Fung.
facts.F9: Mr Fung left the employ of the defendant in March 1989.
facts.F10: On the 24th July 1989, Messrs Fred Kan & Co., solicitors, wrote a letter to the defendant on behalf of Mr Fung informing them that Mr Wong had assigned all his rights under the contract with the defendant to Mr Fung.
facts.F11: The letter reads that the assignment was entered into to secure the performance by Mr Wong of his obligations under a Promissory Note dated 9th day of June, 1989.
facts.F12: The defendant terminated the contract with the plaintiff on the 13th September 1989.
facts.F13: The ICAC reported to have carried out investigations, however, no charge has been preferred against Mr Wong although the investigations are still continuing.
facts.F14: Mr Wong had desperately wanted to retain the contract which was his main source of income.
facts.F15: Mr Wong contended that it was necessary for a solicitor to draw up a contract for the sale of paper when it had never been drawn up in this manner before.

facts.F1: The plaintiff is a company incorporated in Hong Kong on 4 June 1991.
facts.F2: Until 28 March 1995, its shareholders were Gao Yumen (Gao), Tan Bei Lan (Tan) and the defendant, holding 2,500 shares, 5,000 shares and 2,500 shares respectively.
facts.F3: The defendant’s wife and Tan are sisters.
facts.F4: The defendant, Gao, and Tan were also directors of the plaintiff in the periods 24-10-1991 to 28-9-1993.
facts.F5: From 28 September 1993 to 12 January 1994, the defendant’s sister Lau Yee Lin Rosanna was also a director of the plaintiff.
facts.F6: On 28 March 1995, Gao, Tan and the defendant sold their shares in the plaintiff to Yip Wai Ki (Yip) and Ng Man (Ng), who are husband and wife.
facts.F7: Consequently, the shares of Gao were transferred to Ng whereas the shares of Tan and the defendant were transferred to Super Ford International Limited.
facts.F8: Before the transfer, Ng and Yip had been appointed as directors of the plaintiff on 12 January 1994.
facts.F9: In April 1995, Ng and Yip were alerted by the accountant of the plaintiff to irregularities in the account of the plaintiff.
facts.F10: In the light of these, an investigation of the plaintiff’s accounts was carried out.
facts.F11: The present claim is a direct outcome of the investigation.
facts.F12: It relates to two sums of money totalling $2,250,000 that were paid out of the plaintiff’s account in May 1993.
facts.F13: The bank statement and accounting documents of the plaintiff show that on 17 May 1993, the plaintiff withdrew from its bank account with First Pacific Bank a sum of $1 million to purchase a cashier order in the like amount.
facts.F14: The cashier order was made out in favour of Iu Lai & Li, solicitors and notaries (ILL).
facts.F15: The purpose of the withdrawal was described on a petty cash voucher of the plaintiff dated 17 May 1993 as “Temporary payment to Mr Lau”. Mr Lau is a reference to the defendant.
facts.F16: On 22 May 1993, the plaintiff withdrew a sum of $1,250,000 from the same account to purchase another cashier order in the same amount.
facts.F17: The cashier order was also made out to ILL.
facts.F18: A petty cash voucher of the plaintiff dated 22 May 1993 described the purpose of the payment as “Temporary payment to Mr Lau”.
facts.F19: ILL was the solicitor for the vendor, Dunfey Limited, and the confirmor, Soon Chip Chuan Wilbur, in the sale and purchase of various lots of land in D.D. No. 243 at Sai King, New Territories.
facts.F20: The purchaser in the transaction is Sun Fung Limited.
facts.F21: The defendant and a Mr Lau Chun Man Paul were the shareholders and directors of Sun Fung Limited.
facts.F22: The cashier orders were payment of the deposit for the purchase of the land.
facts.F23: The sub-sale and purchase agreement between Mr Soon and Sun Fung Limited was signed on 27 May 2003.
facts.F24: However the assignment to Sun Fung Limited was dated 22 June 1993.
facts.F25: The plaintiff never has any interest in the land.
facts.F26: The plaintiff incurred a $3,600,000 loan from Excellent Fine on about 28 May 1993.
facts.F27: The loan was paid to Saleswin Enterprises Limited on 28 May 1993.
facts.F28: On the same day, a sum of $3,650,000 was received by the plaintiff from Saleswin Enterprises Limited.
facts.F29: Part of the money ($2,250,000) was described as repayment by the defendant of the $2,250,000 advancement, but was in truth no repayment by the defendant.

parties: Plaintiff: The Owners of Cargo Lately Laden on Board the Ship or Vessel ‘BRIJ’, The Owners of Cargo Lately Laden on Board the Ship or Vessel ‘MURTER’, The Owners of Cargo Lately Laden on Board the Ship or Vessel ‘AL SALIMIAH’ (ALL collectively referred to as Glory Products Co. Ltd.)

Defendant: The Owners and/or Demise Charterers of the Ship or Vessel ‘BRIJ’, The Owners and/or Demise Charterers of the Ship or Vessel ‘MURTER’, The Owners and/or Demise Charterers of the Ship or Vessel ‘AL SALIMIAH’ (ALL collectively referred to as Defendants)

facts.F1: The Plaintiff, Glory Products Co. Ltd., was a seller and exporter of garments in Hong Kong for export to South America.
facts.F2: The garments were made in China, put into containers, and then shipped from Chinese ports to Hong Kong where they were transshipped on vessels operated by CAVN (but owned by the Defendants) for carriage from Hong Kong to Venezuela.
facts.F3: The goods in question were sold to buyer, Acetex International SA (Buyer) who operated in the Venezuela ports by its agent Francisco Amaya (Amaya) and its customs agent Oran (Oran).
facts.F4: The Plaintiff effected its shipment of the goods from China to Venezuela by going to a freight forwarder, Wing Tung Wei (China) Ltd. (WTW) which also operated its shipping side under the name of Talent Express Line (Talent).
facts.F5: WTW issued to the Plaintiff, Talent bills of lading, such as the Talent Bills in this case, which were then used by the Plaintiff as documents of title through the bank to obtain payment from the Buyer under the appropriate letters of credit.
facts.F6: Unknown to the Plaintiff, by arrangement between WTW and Hong Kong Maritime Co. Ltd., the Hong Kong agent of CAVN, CAVN issued to WTW as shipper, bills of lading of CAVN evidencing the shipment of the goods to Venezuela corresponding in most particulars to the shipment under the Talent Bills.
facts.F7: The goods arrived in Venezuela and were required under Venezuelan law to be handed to the Venezuelan Customs.
facts.F8: The goods were stored in warehouses controlled by the Venezuelan Customs and were then released by the Venezuelan Customs to Oran, who was acting as customs agent on behalf of Amaya, the Consignee under the CAVN Bills.
facts.F9: The Plaintiff started to make inquiries about the goods long after the delivery of the goods by the Venezuelan Customs to Amaya.
facts.F10: The existence of the CAVN Bills was discovered, and eventually, these proceedings were instituted against the Defendants.
facts.F11: The Plaintiff was not named as Shipper in the CAVN Bills.
facts.F12: The Plaintiff did not know about the existence of the CAVN Bills.
facts.F13: The CAVN Bills were delivered to Amaya in accordance with the contract and not in breach of it.

claim: The plaintiff claims $500,000.00 for the price of goods sold and delivered.
requested_remedy: The plaintiff claims $500,000.00 for the price of goods sold and delivered.

facts.F1: The plaintiff agreed to sell her house to the defendant.
facts.F2: The parties entered into a collateral agreement for the sale and purchase of the house contents at a price of $500,000.00.
facts.F3: The Memorandum of the agreement was signed by both parties and dated 20 February 1992.
facts.F4: The plaintiff let the defendant have the keys to the house before completion.
facts.F5: The defendant made a loan of $300,000.00 to the plaintiff, which was paid off from the proceeds of the sale at the time of completion.
facts.F6: The defendant denied owing the plaintiff $500,000.00 and claimed that the plaintiff failed to deliver the house contents.
facts.F7: The defendant's witnesses, Mr. Lau Yiu Ming and Mr. Hon Pui Kwan, testified that the house was empty when they visited it with the defendant.
facts.F8: The defendant's friend and business partner, Mr. Ko Saheki, testified that he saw the house contents, including antique-style sofas, when he visited the house with the defendant before the sale.
facts.F9: Mr. Ko Saheki also testified that when he visited the house again after the sale, the contents were gone.
facts.F10: The Memorandum did not include an inventory of the house contents.
facts.F11: The plaintiff would not strip the house bare of all contents, including fitted wardrobes and kitchen cabinets.
facts.F12: The Memorandum came into being about 20 February 1992 and not backdated to the time of completion.
facts.F13: The defendant was given the keys to the house some time in March, after the signing of the Sale and Purchase Agreement.

claim: The plaintiff asserts that he slipped and fell and suffered personal injuries that were caused by the negligence of, and breach of duty as occupiers by, the defendants.
requested_remedy: The plaintiff asserts that he slipped and fell and suffered personal injuries that were caused by the negligence of, and breach of duty as occupiers by, the defendants.
parties: Defendant: HONG KONG HOUSING AUTHORITY and KAI FU PROPERTY SERVICES COMPANY LIMITED

facts.F1: The alleged accident occurred on the morning of 24 August 2009 inside the parking area of Sheung Wing House, Upper Ngau Tau Kok Estate.
facts.F2: The plaintiff was employed as a Senior Police Constable by the Hong Kong Police Force and was attached to the Sau Mau Ping District Headquarter Squad 1.
facts.F3: The 1st defendant was responsible for the management of the Upper Ngau Tau Kok Estate, including the place of the alleged accident.
facts.F4: The 2nd defendant was the property management company providing property management services to the Upper Ngau Tau Kok Estate, including the place of the alleged accident.
facts.F5: On the morning of the alleged accident, the plaintiff was on duty and walking across the parking area to the Upper Ngau Tau Kok Temporary Police Station with his colleague.
facts.F6: A plan of the area was produced, showing the path that the plaintiff and his colleague would take to reach the Temporary Police Station.
facts.F7: Photographs were taken of the location, showing a drain covered by a long continuous metal grille.
facts.F8: There were boards placed on the kerb of the pavement to enable wheeled carts to access the pavement from the road surface.
facts.F9: The edges of the boards looked frayed and worse from wear and tear, but the surfaces remained smooth.
facts.F10: There were piles of sand at the end of the car park, and construction work was being carried out at the estate.
facts.F11: A CCTV recording showed the events of the alleged accident, including the plaintiff walking towards the pavement, stepping on one of the boards, and falling forward.
facts.F12: The plaintiff did not get up after falling and was later taken to the hospital.
facts.F13: The plaintiff gave a statement to the police on 15 January 2010, stating that he stepped onto something on the kerb and fell, and had not lost consciousness.
facts.F14: The plaintiff's left foot did not slip on the board, but rather his right foot gave way as he was stepping forward.
facts.F15: The plaintiff had back problems and issues with his superiors, which raised suspicion about the accidental nature of his fall.

claim: claims for return of the balance of deposit in the sum of $280,729
requested_remedy: claims for return of the balance of deposit in the sum of $280,729
parties: Defendant: Hing Yip Investment Company Limited And Fervent Estate Limited

facts.F1: The Plaintiff rented the Ground Floor and the basement of Full Win Commercial Centre, No. 573 Nathan Road, from the Defendants as landlord, for the period from 15 August 2000 to 14 August 2003, at a monthly rent of $130,000.
facts.F2: The Plaintiff yielded up the Premises to the Defendant on 14 August 2003.
facts.F3: The Defendant deducted a sum of $280,729 from the deposit, and only returned to the Plaintiff on 11 September 2003 the balance of the deposit in the sum of $251,003.
facts.F4: When the Plaintiff surrendered the Premises to the Defendant, the following items of works had been done: (1) Alterations and/or additions to fire service installations of Defendants in the Premises including 50 heat detectors, 50 remote controlled lights, 1 set of fire alarm, 108 fire sprinklers and 1 set of fire hose (the Fire Services Work); (2) Demolition of 2 toilets, i.e. the toilet for the disabled (with water closet and wash basin) and the male toilet (with water closet, wash basin and male lavatory), removal of wash basins in the female toilet and installation of another water closet thereon; (3) Raised flooring by concrete of 6 inches thick embedded with water and drainage pipes on the area coloured pink on Exhibit D1; (4) Demolition of 2 walls (including 2 doors) next to the staircase leading from the Ground Floor portion to the Basement portion of the Premises.
facts.F5: The cost of repairing and reinstating the fire services installations is $27,000. The cost of repairing and reinstating 3 toilets and 2 walls next to the staircase is $103,700. The cost of reinstating the floor is $58,000. The loss of use and occupation of the Premises required for the execution of the reinstatement works rental for 20 days at $92,029, based on estimated market rental of $110,000, and air-conditioning charges and management fees at $28,044 per month.
facts.F6: The Plaintiff delivered the Premises with only 3 partitions, each of which had a water closet, after demolishing 2 smaller toilets and converting the wash basins area in the larger toilet into another partition with a water closet.
facts.F7: The Premises should have been delivered by the Plaintiff in a bare shell condition, meaning unfurnished and undecorated, as per the meaning of 'bare' in the Shorter Oxford English Dictionary.
facts.F8: Only the Fire Services Work which cost $27,000 was carried out as reinstatement work by the Defendant.
facts.F9: The direct losses and damages sustained or incurred by the Defendant due to the Plaintiff's breach of the Lease amount to $68,413.20.

facts.F9: The Partnership Agreement provided that they would share the expenses/profits in equal shares.
facts.F10: Mr. Yip and his workers were engaged by Mr. Fan to transport construction materials from the Helipad to the Site via the Peak.
facts.F11: The farmer trailers provided by Mr. Fan broke down from time to time, and Mr. Yip and his workers threatened not to carry on with their work any further because it was impracticable to transport further construction materials to the Site without conveyance.
facts.F12: Mr. Fan was responsible to transport all construction materials, construction tools/machineries, and arrange water supply to the Site.
facts.F13: Mr. Fan was responsible to provide man power to transport the structural parts of the pavilion.

claim: The plaintiff claims $25,000.00 being one month’s salary in lieu of notice; $15,927.00 being pro-rata a 13th month’s salary; and an account of all sums due and owing by the defendant by way of commission of 10% payable to the plaintiff.
requested_remedy: The plaintiff claims $25,000.00 being one month’s salary in lieu of notice; $15,927.00 being pro-rata a 13th month’s salary; and an account of all sums due and owing by the defendant by way of commission of 10% payable to the plaintiff.

facts.F1: The plaintiff resigned from his previous employer, Alan Development, in July 1993 and joined the defendant's company in October 1993.
facts.F2: The plaintiff's employment contract with the defendant was not in writing, but the terms were discussed and agreed upon over dinner on 30th September 1993.
facts.F3: The defendant's director, Mr. Depardieu, illustrated the terms on the back of his business card, which included a salary of $25,000.00 per month and a possible bonus at Chinese New Year.
facts.F4: The plaintiff received no commission of 10% on account profits, and when he inquired about it, Mr. Depardieu said there was not yet any profit.
facts.F5: In August 1994, the plaintiff had a discussion with Mr. Depardieu and Mrs. Lin, the other director of the defendant, about varying his terms of employment.
facts.F6: The plaintiff left the office after the meeting, and the defendant prepared a confirmatory letter and a cheque for the plaintiff, which the plaintiff refused to accept.
facts.F7: The plaintiff claimed that he was terminated without notice, while the defendant claimed that the plaintiff resigned.
facts.F8: The plaintiff was appointed as a manager in the defendant based on the agreed terms.
facts.F9: A confirmatory letter and a cheque were prepared by the defendant after the meeting with the plaintiff in August 1994.
